Extra Calvinisticum
EK-strah kal-vin-IS-ti-kum
noun (Reformed Christology)
Latin: the Calvinistic beyond (a term coined by Lutheran opponents). The Reformed Christological doctrine that the eternal Son, in the incarnation, was united to but not confined within the human nature — the Son continued to fill and uphold the universe even while incarnate (the Son existing also beyond or outside the flesh, etiam extra carnem).

📖 Biblical Definition

Latin for the Calvinistic beyond / outside (a term coined by Lutheran opponents in the Reformed-Lutheran Christological controversies); the Reformed Christological doctrine that the eternal Son, in the incarnation, was united to but not confined within or exhausted by the human nature. The doctrine holds that the eternal Son, while truly and personally united to the human nature in the incarnation, continued to exist and act also beyond (extra) the human nature — continuing to fill heaven and earth, to uphold all things by the word of His power, to be omnipresent according to His divine nature — even during His incarnate life on earth. The Son was not so confined within the human body that He ceased His cosmic divine operations; the infinite divine nature is not contained or circumscribed by the finite human nature. The doctrine is grounded in: (1) the immensity and omnipresence of the divine nature, which cannot be confined to one location (Jeremiah 23:24; the divine nature fills heaven and earth); (2) Colossians 1:17, by him all things consist (the Son upholds the universe, a cosmic operation that did not cease during the incarnation); (3) John 3:13, the Son of man which is in heaven (the Son of Man spoken of as in heaven even while on earth, in the Person who unites the two natures); (4) Hebrews 1:3, the Son upholding all things by the word of His power. Though called the extra Calvinisticum by Lutheran opponents (who, holding the ubiquity of Christ's body for their consubstantiation doctrine, objected to it), the doctrine is in fact the catholic Christological position held by the Fathers (Athanasius, Augustine, Cyril) and the medieval theologians, not a Calvinist innovation. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: the eternal Son, in the incarnation, was truly and personally united to the human nature without being confined within it; even while incarnate, He continued to fill and uphold the universe according to His divine nature. The doctrine preserves the integrity of both natures (the infinite divine nature not confined by the finite human nature; the finite human nature not made omnipresent) and undergirds the Reformed spiritual-presence doctrine of the Lord's Supper (against the Lutheran ubiquity-of-Christ's-body).

EXTRA CALVINISTICUM, n. (Reformed Christology; Latin, the Calvinistic beyond/outside, coined by Lutheran opponents) The eternal Son, in the incarnation, was truly and personally united to but not confined within the human nature; He continued to exist and act also beyond (extra) the flesh — filling heaven and earth, upholding all things, omnipresent according to His divine nature — even during His incarnate life. The infinite divine nature is not contained by the finite human nature. Grounded in: divine immensity (Jeremiah 23:24); Colossians 1:17 (by him all things consist); John 3:13 (the Son of man which is in heaven); Hebrews 1:3. In fact the catholic Christological position (Athanasius, Augustine, Cyril), not a Calvinist innovation. Preserves the integrity of both natures; undergirds the Reformed Supper doctrine.

📖 Key Scripture

John 3:13 — "And no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven."

Colossians 1:17 — "And he is before all things, and by him all things consist."

Hebrews 1:3 — "Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power."

Jeremiah 23:24 — "Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? saith the LORD. Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the LORD."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The extra Calvinisticum is in fact the catholic Christological position (not a Calvinist innovation); it is opposed by the Lutheran ubiquity-of-Christ's-body doctrine, which holds the divine nature so communicated its omnipresence to the human nature that Christ's body is everywhere present.

expand to see more

The extra Calvinisticum is in fact the catholic Christological position held by the Fathers and the medieval theologians, despite its name (coined polemically by Lutheran opponents). It is opposed principally by the Lutheran doctrine of the ubiquity of Christ's body, developed to undergird the Lutheran consubstantiation doctrine of the Lord's Supper. The Lutheran position holds that through the communication of attributes (communicatio idiomatum) the divine attribute of omnipresence is so communicated to Christ's human nature that His body is everywhere present, enabling its bodily presence in, with, and under the elements at every celebration of the Supper. The Reformed extra Calvinisticum holds the opposite: the communication of attributes operates at the level of the Person (the one Person possesses the attributes of both natures), but the attributes of one nature are not transferred to the other nature; the divine nature retains its omnipresence and the human nature retains its finite locality; the eternal Son is united to the human nature without the human nature being made omnipresent, and continues to fill and uphold the universe according to His divine nature even while the human nature is locally embodied. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive extra Calvinisticum: the eternal Son, in the incarnation, was united to but not confined within the human nature; even while incarnate, He continued to fill and uphold the cosmos according to His divine nature (Colossians 1:17; Hebrews 1:3); the doctrine preserves the integrity of both natures and undergirds the Reformed spiritual-presence doctrine of the Supper (Christ's body remaining in heaven, the believer's heart lifted up by the Spirit to commune with Him) against the Lutheran ubiquity doctrine.
